overview: Mapuche communities have a long history across parts of present-day Chile and Argentina. The map shows only a brief interval during nineteenth-century invasions of their territories. Local communities and leaders formed changing alliances; they were not one uniform kingdom.

periods.title: Autonomy and changing connections
periods.summary: Mapuche communities resisted, negotiated and adapted through frontier contact.

periods.title: Military occupation in Araucanía
periods.summary: Chilean military expansion culminated in occupation and the confinement of communities to reduced lands.

items.text: The ruka is a place for household life, work and community gatherings. Its hearth connects cooking with conversation, and activities such as weaving and basketry can share the same interior. The museum stresses that home design must make room for these living practices.

Historical accounts describe different family arrangements rather than one standard household. Some nineteenth-century polygamous families had several hearths within a ruka. Hearths can therefore tell a social story as well as a story about keeping warm and preparing food.

Pascual Coña recalled house-building as a community undertaking. A respected neighbour organized workers, who gathered timber and vines to bind the frame. Building a home called for cooperation and practical knowledge of local materials.

Food was part of that work. Coña’s account describes drinks, mote and meat prepared for the people building the house, followed by eating and conversation around the hearth. The housewarming began with the people who had actually helped raise the house.

Palin brings communities together through play, food and discussion. It can carry political, spiritual and social purposes as well as competition. Families and visitors help make the event, so the important activity extends well beyond the players holding sticks.

A traditional pali ball could be shaped from a rounded growth on a tree, then scraped into a sphere. Other versions used wool and coverings. Makers adapted materials while preserving a game in which players drive the ball toward the opposite end.

A single-log canoe was recovered from Lake Lanalhue in 1995. The museum displays the hollowed trunk but does not give a secure construction date in this account. Its surviving wood is direct evidence of skilled water transport in the region.

Community research connects these canoes with exchange, kinship and friendship between settlements. A water route could carry goods and knowledge together. Recalling the boats also helps explain how the coastal territory was connected before many journeys moved onto roads.

Pascual Coña narrated his life to a missionary in the 1920s, looking back at the nineteenth century. The resulting text preserves a Mapuche voice through the work of a transcriber. It is invaluable, but readers should remember how the spoken account became a book.

Chile’s national library preserves a photograph of a girl and young woman beside a loom, dated around 1860. It records people and weaving equipment close to this map’s period. Like many early photographs, its posed arrangement is part of the evidence.

In Marjorie Huaiqui Hernández’s modern story, a child says “Wanglen pigen iñche”, meaning “My name is Wanglen”. The printed Mapudungun appears on page 87 of Palabras de tierra y sol. This is an actual contemporary literary sample, not invented dialogue for an ancient person.

Chilean troops suppressed the major 1881 to 1882 uprising and completed their planned occupation campaign in 1883. New land arrangements impoverished many communities and restricted their autonomy. The map’s 1880 cutoff falls before this decisive stage of conquest.

ending.text: Mapuche political autonomy and landholding suffered greatly under nineteenth-century military conquest and settlement. The people did not disappear: communities, Mapudungun, cultural work and new political strategies continued. The imported 1880 endpoint is neither their beginning nor their end.
